# Claude Memory Compiler Setup

On 2026-04-14, the `coleam00/claude-memory-compiler` system — the same daily-log-to-knowledge-base architecture this very knowledge base runs on — was installed to give Claude Code persistent memory across sessions. The repo was cloned to `~/.claude/claude-memory-compiler/`, Python dependencies installed via `uv sync`, and the knowledge base directory structure (`daily/`, `knowledge/concepts/`, etc.) initialized. This system is Tier C of a three-tier Claude Code memory architecture; see [[concepts/claude-code-memory-architecture]] for the full picture including Tier A (native auto-memory) and Tier B (custom Stop-hook scratchpad). On 2026-06-13, a day-long failure caused by `claude-agent-sdk` version skew revealed an important operational maintenance pattern.

## Key Points

- Three global hooks were wired into `~/.claude/settings.json`: `session-start.py` (SessionStart), `session-end.py` (SessionEnd), and `pre-compact.py` (PreCompact).
- Hook commands invoke `uv` via its absolute path (`~/.local/bin/uv`) rather than the bare `uv` command, because Claude Code's hook execution environment may not include `~/.local/bin` on `PATH`.
- All script invocations follow the `uv run --directory ~/.claude/claude-memory-compiler <script>` pattern, guaranteeing the correct virtualenv context regardless of the current working directory when a hook fires.
- Hook configuration changes are not picked up live — they require a full Claude Code restart (or a `/hooks` reload) before they take effect.
- After 6 PM local time, the `flush.py` background process automatically triggers `compile.py` to turn that day's daily log into knowledge articles, without manual intervention. Manual queries are also available via `uv run --directory ~/.claude/claude-memory-compiler python scripts/query.py "<question>"`.
- **The agent itself never receives a "session ending" notification** — SessionEnd and PreCompact are harness-level events; the harness runs the hook shell commands, not the agent. Teardown logic must live in the hook, not in agent-side instructions.
- **Version skew failure mode:** the memory compiler's `uv` virtualenv pins `claude-agent-sdk` to a specific version, which bundles a specific Claude Code CLI binary. When the system Claude Code auto-updates (e.g., from 2.1.92 to 2.1.177), the bundled CLI in the venv falls behind and eventually cannot parse the current `~/.claude/settings.json`, causing every `flush.py` invocation to exit immediately with a non-zero code. Symptom: 100% FLUSH_ERROR rate after a Claude Code update, despite no changes to the memory compiler itself.
- **Fix for version skew:** `cd ~/.claude/claude-memory-compiler && uv lock --upgrade-package claude-agent-sdk && uv sync`. This upgrades only the `claude-agent-sdk` dependency and its bundled CLI to match the current system version without touching other pinned dependencies. Run this whenever FLUSH_ERRORs appear after a Claude Code auto-update.
- **Diagnostic caution:** do NOT invoke the bundled `claude.exe` CLI directly to diagnose version skew — it spawns a real nested agent session. Instead, inspect venv package metadata (e.g., `uv pip show claude-agent-sdk`) to check the installed version against the system CLI version.

## Details

The setup session focused on making the memory pipeline reliable rather than merely functional. The PATH issue with `uv` is a generalizable lesson for any Claude Code hook that shells out to a tool installed via `uv`, `pipx`, or similar user-local installers: hook processes may run with a minimal environment, so absolute paths (or explicit `PATH` exports) are safer than relying on the interactive shell's configuration. Similarly, the `uv run --directory` pattern avoids a whole class of "wrong virtualenv" bugs that would otherwise occur if a hook fires while Claude Code's working directory is some unrelated project.

Once restarted, the three hooks form a closed loop: `session-start.py` injects the current knowledge index and the most recent daily log into every new session's context (capped at 20,000 characters), `session-end.py` and `pre-compact.py` capture the raw conversation transcript and spawn a detached `flush.py` process, and `flush.py` decides what's worth appending to the day's daily log and, after 6 PM, kicks off `compile.py` to synthesize that log into structured `knowledge/` articles. PreCompact serves as a safety net for long sessions: in a session with multiple auto-compactions, PreCompact fires before each one, ensuring at least one compiled log exists even if the session later crashes before SessionEnd fires.

The 2026-06-13 version skew failure is operationally important. On that day, Claude Code auto-updated from approximately version 2.1.92 to 2.1.177 — 85 releases ahead — while the memory compiler's venv still bundled the older CLI via `claude-agent-sdk==0.1.56`. The newer `~/.claude/settings.json` included hooks, settings, or schemas added after version 2.1.92 that the stale bundled CLI could not parse; every `flush.py` call exited on startup without processing the session. The failure was isolated entirely to the Tier C compile layer: Tier B (the `transcript-capture.js` Stop-hook) continued capturing sessions uninterrupted because it has no dependency on `claude-agent-sdk`. Twenty-four days of continuous Tier B logs and four sessions captured on the failure day itself confirmed the architectural independence. This means that during a version-skew failure, raw session context is preserved in Tier B transcripts and can be backfilled after the fix is applied. The `uv lock --upgrade-package claude-agent-sdk && uv sync` fix is surgical — it upgrades only the affected package without touching other pinned dependencies — and is safe to apply at any time. A post-fix test flush verifies the fix before trusting that normal operation has resumed. See [[connections/memory-compiler-tier-independence-under-failure]] for the architectural insight this failure demonstrated empirically.

# Session Context Footprint Audit (doctor-plus)

The audit returned 3 FLAG / 3 PASS across six "then-and-now" context-engineering shifts. ## Key Points

- **~21.5k tokens always loaded at session start** versus a stated ~3,000 in `CLAUDE.md`. The ~7,640-token floor (guidance files plus memory-compiler injection) is directly measured; the skill-description totals that make up the remainder are approximate.

- **A single scaled stacked bar with a dashed marker at the claimed 3,000-token budget** made the stated-versus-measured gap legible at a glance, replacing a table the reader would otherwise have to parse.

# In-Session Background Processes Don't Survive; Hours-Scale Work Belongs in Scheduled Jobs

Long-running background processes started from within a Claude Code session do not reliably survive the session — when the session ends they are terminated (status `killed`), and any child work they spawned can be left orphaned. On 2026-07-27, this was demonstrated when foreground memsearch reindex tasks were killed twice, leaving orphaned indexer processes that had to be cleaned up. The architectural conclusion: work measured in hours (like a first-time embedding index) belongs in a scheduled OS-level job, not an in-session background command.

## Key Points

- **Session-scoped processes are killed with the session:** a background command launched inside a session shares the session's lifetime; when the session terminates, the process is killed (observed status `killed`), regardless of whether its work completed.
- **Killed background jobs can orphan children:** the 2026-07-27 reindex tasks were killed twice, each time leaving orphaned indexer processes still holding CPU that had to be manually cleaned up — a killed parent does not guarantee a clean child teardown.
- **Hours-scale work must be relocated to a scheduled job:** a first-time SecondBrain book-library index is an hours-scale job (one indexer burned 81 CPU-minutes and was still going); the correct home is a Windows scheduled task (the 6:15 AM `daily-backup.ps1`), which runs independently of any session.
- **Sessions cannot wait through discontinuities:** a session cannot wait through a machine restart, nor block for hours on an index; the general workaround is to hand the work to a scheduled task and surface results/failures asynchronously (e.g., via `.errors.log` escalation read at the next session start).

## Details

The failure is structural, not incidental. A Claude Code session's process tree is tied to the session's lifetime, so any background command it launches is a candidate for termination when the session ends or is interrupted. This is acceptable for short tasks that finish within a turn, but it is fundamentally mismatched to work whose runtime exceeds a session — an hours-scale first-time embedding index cannot complete before the session that started it is likely gone. Worse, a killed background parent does not guarantee its own descendants are reaped: on 2026-07-27 the killed reindex tasks left orphaned indexer processes consuming CPU, requiring an explicit cleanup pass. The lesson is that the session is the wrong execution context for durable, long-running work.

The remedy is to move such work to an OS-level scheduler that owns its own lifetime and execution ceiling — in this case the nightly 6:15 AM backup task, which runs uncapped by the session, with an execution limit widened (30 min → 2 h) to absorb a heavy reindex night. This is the same reasoning that motivates the self-deleting post-restart health-check task: since a session cannot literally wait through a reboot, a logon-triggered scheduled task performs the post-restart verification and escalates failures asynchronously. In both cases the pattern is identical — take work that outlives or straddles a session boundary, hand it to a scheduled task, and reconcile the outcome later through a durable artifact (a log, an alarm counter, an escalation file) rather than expecting the session to hold state across the gap.

# Connection: An Error Names the Transport, Not the Cause

## The Connection

Two findings from 2026-10-03 fail in the same way at opposite ends of the stack. A `memsearch-sync` hook reported a gRPC `_InactiveRpcError`; the actual cause was that Docker Desktop was not running, so Milvus was down and there was nothing on the other end of the connection ([[concepts/memsearch-indexing-lock-docker-dependency]]). A `status-report` probe raised a regex error; the actual cause was that `subprocess.run(..., text=True)` had decoded Chrome's UTF-8 output as CP1252, returned `None`, and handed that `None` to the regex ([[concepts/python-default-encoding-subprocess-windows]]). In each case the message accurately describes the layer where execution stopped and says nothing about the layer that caused it.

This is already the established reading of memsearch timeouts, where three separate causes — oversized context, a bad embedded Python path, and a stopped Docker container — all presented identically ([[concepts/memsearch-tool-maintenance]]), and of background-job notifications, where an apparent failure was a host memory-pressure reap rather than a defect ([[concepts/background-job-reaped-memory-pressure]]).

## Key Insight

The diagnostic value of an error message is bounded by what the erroring layer can observe, and a layer can only observe its own immediate input. gRPC knows the socket was inactive; it cannot know that a container manager is stopped two levels down. A regex knows it received a non-string; it cannot know that a locale encoding mismatch three statements earlier produced it. So the message reliably identifies *where to start walking*, and reliably misidentifies *what to fix* — which is why both of these would have led a reader straight to the wrong file. The regex looks like the bug. The memsearch code looks like the bug.

The practical consequence is a rule about ordering: walk the dependency chain downward from the error before reading any implementation. For memsearch that chain is short and cheap — is Docker up, is Milvus healthy, does a trivial search return, does a scheduled task already hold the lock — and in both 2026-10-03 cases checking it cost less than reading the code would have. A second, subtler consequence concerns exit codes and generic failures: `memsearch-drain.ps1` exiting 1 after a twenty-minute wait is not a crash but a second run losing the indexing lock, and a reaped background job is a resource event. Both are *correct* behavior reported through a channel that can only express failure. Treating a generic failure signal as a question — what else was true at that moment? — rather than as an answer is what separates the five-minute diagnosis from the afternoon spent debugging a healthy component.

## Evidence

- 2026-10-03 (07:58): "Docker Desktop down ⇒ Milvus down ⇒ memsearch hooks fail with gRPC errors. First thing to check on a memsearch hook failure." Starting Docker restored Milvus to healthy and a test search returned results immediately.
- 2026-10-03 (07:58): `memsearch-drain.ps1` exit code 1 after ~20 minutes was the lock being held by the 7:33 AM scheduled task (PID 27824) — "not a real failure."
- 2026-10-03 (18:16): "this laptop's Python defaults to CP1252, so Chrome's UTF-8 output fails to decode, stdout comes back `None`, and the regex then errors." The surfaced error was the regex, three statements downstream of the decode.
- 2026-09-30: a memsearch timeout traced to a stopped Docker Milvus container, establishing that "timeouts are nearly uninformative about cause, so check the dependency chain first."
- 2026-09-24: a background job's termination notification was a memory-pressure reap, "a resource event, not a failure to debug."

## The Connection

Both substantive sessions on 2026-04-22 ran into a version of the same problem: a tool or agent produced output that *looked* fine - a citation with a plausible author list, a photo wired into HTML with a correct relative path - but was actually wrong or unverifiable through the usual checking method. # SportScienceResearchRepo Batch PDF Import Pipeline

SportScienceResearchRepo maintains a `papers.json` database of sports-science research papers, built up through an ongoing batch-import campaign that processes a large backlog of football-related PDFs in rounds. On 2026-04-21, round 7 used 10 parallel subagents to add papers with IDs 334-383 to the database. A follow-up session on 2026-04-22 resolved a set of `year: 0`/blank-data quality issues left over from earlier rounds, including two that round 7 itself had flagged.

## Key Points

- Each import round assigns a contiguous block of IDs (round 7: 334-383, 50 papers) across 10 parallel subagents, with each agent handling a 5-paper batch.
- Before writing agent prompts for a new round, the format/schema is confirmed against a recently-completed batch file to keep entries consistent across rounds.
- Agents complete in non-sequential order; completions are tracked individually (round 7: agents 1, 2, 3, 5, 7, 8, 9 finished first, with agents 4, 6, and 10 still outstanding) before a separate "merge agent" consolidates all 10 batch files into `papers.json` and pushes the result.

- On 2026-04-22, a repair session fixed 6 entries with `year: 0`/blank data carried over from earlier rounds: IDs 286 and 287 (true duplicates), 292 and 294 (unreadable filenames), 336 (a misassigned URL, recataloged from an ankle-sprain paper to Xia et al. 2024 on gut microbiota), and 358 (the KIAA0319 paper, originally blocked by non-breaking spaces in its filename) - resolving both of the data-quality issues round 7 had flagged (336 and 358).

The batch-import campaign works through a large backlog of football-related research PDFs in fixed-size rounds, each adding 50 papers via 10 parallel 5-paper agent batches. This parallelization lets a round's worth of extraction work happen concurrently, but it also means completion tracking has to happen at the individual-agent level - in round 7, seven of the ten agents (1, 2, 3, 5, 7, 8, 9) finished before the remaining three (4, 6, 10), and the round could not be merged until all ten reported done. Once all batch files are complete, a dedicated merge agent consolidates them into the shared `papers.json` and pushes the update, advancing the repo's paper count (333 -> 383 after round 7).

ID 358 could not be matched to any PDF on disk and was marked `"SOURCE FILE UNREADABLE"` per schema rather than skipped entirely. ID 336's source PDF had a curly apostrophe in its filename (URL-encoded as `%E2%80%99` in its `driveUrl`), which prevented the file from being read - this was logged as an open issue to investigate and fix rather than resolved inline. ID 343's PDF was misnamed "NFL Play Smart" but actually contained an unrelated hamstring-injury paper (Vermeulen et al.), requiring the agent to catalog it under its true content rather than its filename. ID 340 (Dupont et al., on lumbar disk herniation) used a Wolters Kluwer "in-press" DOI format whose final form was uncertain, so it was flagged for staff verification rather than guessed at. Together these conventions - explicit "unreadable" markers, content-based (not filename-based) cataloging, and flagging-for-review rather than guessing - keep the dataset complete and auditable even when individual source files are problematic.

The 2026-04-22 session closed out exactly the two issues round 7 had flagged - ID 358 (unreadable filename) and ID 336 (curly-apostrophe filename/misassigned URL) - alongside four additional `year: 0`/blank entries (286, 287, 292, 294) discovered separately. # Statistical Inference Audit Checklist for Evidence Briefs

The 2026-09-18 adversarial audit of the TOS evidence brief surfaced a reusable set of inferential error patterns that recur whenever a literature review is turned into practice recommendations. The unifying diagnosis was that sources and study-level numbers were largely correct while the *last inferential step* — from observation to causal, screening, or policy claim — was not. The patterns below function as a checklist for auditing any similar brief.

## Key Points

- **Descriptive → causal/screening drift.** The dominant failure: a correlational or descriptive finding is restated as a reason to screen, intervene, or set policy. Check every recommendation against what its cited study design can actually license.
- **"No significant difference" ≠ equivalence.** A null significance test in a small, non-equivalence-designed trial (the cited tennis study had n=10) establishes only that the study lacked power to detect a difference. It is not a safety finding and cannot exonerate an exposure.
- **Reliability/normative data ≠ screening validity.** Datasets establishing that a measure is consistent (pec minor length, DNF, SME, CKCUEST, UQYBT) say nothing about whether that measure predicts the condition of interest.
- **Same-cohort derivation and testing invalidates a cut-point.** An n=49 threshold derived and then tested in the same cohort, with a relative-risk CI of 1.28–68.49, is not a validated screen; the CI width alone signals near-zero information about effect size.
- **Denominator and magnitude hygiene.** Do not juxtapose incompatible denominators (annual incidence vs. 7-year cumulative prevalence). Recompute rhetorical magnitude claims: "four orders of magnitude" for 8.6% vs. 0.004% is actually ~3.33 (ratio ≈ 2,143).
- **Borrowed population rates cannot be applied and then waived.** Using a general-population incidence for an athlete cohort and then dismissing the implication is incoherent — either use an athlete-specific model or state that the expected rate is unknown.

## Details

Two of the patterns deserve particular attention because they are easy to state backwards. The first is the cluster-plausibility argument. Under a Poisson model with the brief's own assumed 4/100,000/yr incidence, a 35-athlete season gives λ = 0.0014, so P(≥2 cases) ≈ 0.000000979 — meaning the model the brief invoked to reassure actually implies the observed two-case cluster is extraordinary. The brief then compounded this by placing a confidence interval around the *observed* event count and using its width as evidence of plausibility; a CI on observed events characterizes uncertainty in the estimate, not surprisingness under an assumed rate, so it answers a different question than the one posed. When a reassurance argument is constructed post hoc, it is worth checking whether the model actually supports the reassurance or contradicts it.

The second is the use of a study design outside the inferential range it supports. A cross-sectional biopsy taken *after* disease onset cannot establish what did or did not cause the disease, yet it was used to exonerate the weight room as a contributing exposure — a temporality violation that no amount of sample size fixes. The same class of error underlies the reliability-as-validity mistake: the studies are real and well-conducted, but they answer "is this measurement repeatable?" rather than "does this measurement predict TOS?", and only the latter licenses a screen. The practical audit procedure that surfaced all of these is a claim-by-claim verification table: for each assertion in the document, record the source, the number as stated in the source, the number as stated in the brief, and — critically — whether the study design supports the inferential use being made. Most rows will pass the first three columns; the fourth is where the findings cluster.

# Claude Memory Compiler Setup

On 2026-04-14, the `coleam00/claude-memory-compiler` system — the same daily-log-to-knowledge-base architecture this very knowledge base runs on — was installed to give Claude Code persistent memory across sessions. The repo was cloned to `~/.claude/claude-memory-compiler/`, Python dependencies installed via `uv sync`, and the knowledge base directory structure (`daily/`, `knowledge/concepts/`, etc.) initialized. This system is Tier C of a three-tier Claude Code memory architecture; see [[concepts/claude-code-memory-architecture]] for the full picture including Tier A (native auto-memory) and Tier B (custom Stop-hook scratchpad). On 2026-06-13, a day-long failure caused by `claude-agent-sdk` version skew revealed an important operational maintenance pattern.

## Key Points

- Three global hooks were wired into `~/.claude/settings.json`: `session-start.py` (SessionStart), `session-end.py` (SessionEnd), and `pre-compact.py` (PreCompact).
- Hook commands invoke `uv` via its absolute path (`~/.local/bin/uv`) rather than the bare `uv` command, because Claude Code's hook execution environment may not include `~/.local/bin` on `PATH`.
- All script invocations follow the `uv run --directory ~/.claude/claude-memory-compiler <script>` pattern, guaranteeing the correct virtualenv context regardless of the current working directory when a hook fires.
- Hook configuration changes are not picked up live — they require a full Claude Code restart (or a `/hooks` reload) before they take effect.
- After 6 PM local time, the `flush.py` background process automatically triggers `compile.py` to turn that day's daily log into knowledge articles, without manual intervention. Manual queries are also available via `uv run --directory ~/.claude/claude-memory-compiler python scripts/query.py "<question>"`.
- **The agent itself never receives a "session ending" notification** — SessionEnd and PreCompact are harness-level events; the harness runs the hook shell commands, not the agent. Teardown logic must live in the hook, not in agent-side instructions.
- **Version skew failure mode:** the memory compiler's `uv` virtualenv pins `claude-agent-sdk` to a specific version, which bundles a specific Claude Code CLI binary. When the system Claude Code auto-updates (e.g., from 2.1.92 to 2.1.177), the bundled CLI in the venv falls behind and eventually cannot parse the current `~/.claude/settings.json`, causing every `flush.py` invocation to exit immediately with a non-zero code. Symptom: 100% FLUSH_ERROR rate after a Claude Code update, despite no changes to the memory compiler itself.
- **Fix for version skew:** `cd ~/.claude/claude-memory-compiler && uv lock --upgrade-package claude-agent-sdk && uv sync`. This upgrades only the `claude-agent-sdk` dependency and its bundled CLI to match the current system version without touching other pinned dependencies. Run this whenever FLUSH_ERRORs appear after a Claude Code auto-update.
- **Diagnostic caution:** do NOT invoke the bundled `claude.exe` CLI directly to diagnose version skew — it spawns a real nested agent session. Instead, inspect venv package metadata (e.g., `uv pip show claude-agent-sdk`) to check the installed version against the system CLI version.

## Details

The setup session focused on making the memory pipeline reliable rather than merely functional. ## Key Points

# In-Session Background Processes Don't Survive; Hours-Scale Work Belongs in Scheduled Jobs

Long-running background processes started from within a Claude Code session do not reliably survive the session — when the session ends they are terminated (status `killed`), and any child work they spawned can be left orphaned. On 2026-07-27, this was demonstrated when foreground memsearch reindex tasks were killed twice, leaving orphaned indexer processes that had to be cleaned up. The architectural conclusion: work measured in hours (like a first-time embedding index) belongs in a scheduled OS-level job, not an in-session background command.

## Key Points

- **Session-scoped processes are killed with the session:** a background command launched inside a session shares the session's lifetime; when the session terminates, the process is killed (observed status `killed`), regardless of whether its work completed.
- **Killed background jobs can orphan children:** the 2026-07-27 reindex tasks were killed twice, each time leaving orphaned indexer processes still holding CPU that had to be manually cleaned up — a killed parent does not guarantee a clean child teardown.
- **Hours-scale work must be relocated to a scheduled job:** a first-time SecondBrain book-library index is an hours-scale job (one indexer burned 81 CPU-minutes and was still going); the correct home is a Windows scheduled task (the 6:15 AM `daily-backup.ps1`), which runs independently of any session.
- **Sessions cannot wait through discontinuities:** a session cannot wait through a machine restart, nor block for hours on an index; the general workaround is to hand the work to a scheduled task and surface results/failures asynchronously (e.g., via `.errors.log` escalation read at the next session start).

## Details

The failure is structural, not incidental. A Claude Code session's process tree is tied to the session's lifetime, so any background command it launches is a candidate for termination when the session ends or is interrupted. This is acceptable for short tasks that finish within a turn, but it is fundamentally mismatched to work whose runtime exceeds a session — an hours-scale first-time embedding index cannot complete before the session that started it is likely gone. Worse, a killed background parent does not guarantee its own descendants are reaped: on 2026-07-27 the killed reindex tasks left orphaned indexer processes consuming CPU, requiring an explicit cleanup pass. The lesson is that the session is the wrong execution context for durable, long-running work.

The remedy is to move such work to an OS-level scheduler that owns its own lifetime and execution ceiling — in this case the nightly 6:15 AM backup task, which runs uncapped by the session, with an execution limit widened (30 min → 2 h) to absorb a heavy reindex night. This is the same reasoning that motivates the self-deleting post-restart health-check task: since a session cannot literally wait through a reboot, a logon-triggered scheduled task performs the post-restart verification and escalates failures asynchronously. In both cases the pattern is identical — take work that outlives or straddles a session boundary, hand it to a scheduled task, and reconcile the outcome later through a durable artifact (a log, an alarm counter, an escalation file) rather than expecting the session to hold state across the gap.

# Connection: An Error Names the Transport, Not the Cause

## The Connection

Two findings from 2026-10-03 fail in the same way at opposite ends of the stack. A `memsearch-sync` hook reported a gRPC `_InactiveRpcError`; the actual cause was that Docker Desktop was not running, so Milvus was down and there was nothing on the other end of the connection ([[concepts/memsearch-indexing-lock-docker-dependency]]). A `status-report` probe raised a regex error; the actual cause was that `subprocess.run(..., text=True)` had decoded Chrome's UTF-8 output as CP1252, returned `None`, and handed that `None` to the regex ([[concepts/python-default-encoding-subprocess-windows]]). In each case the message accurately describes the layer where execution stopped and says nothing about the layer that caused it.

This is already the established reading of memsearch timeouts, where three separate causes — oversized context, a bad embedded Python path, and a stopped Docker container — all presented identically ([[concepts/memsearch-tool-maintenance]]), and of background-job notifications, where an apparent failure was a host memory-pressure reap rather than a defect ([[concepts/background-job-reaped-memory-pressure]]).

## Key Insight

The diagnostic value of an error message is bounded by what the erroring layer can observe, and a layer can only observe its own immediate input. gRPC knows the socket was inactive; it cannot know that a container manager is stopped two levels down. A regex knows it received a non-string; it cannot know that a locale encoding mismatch three statements earlier produced it. So the message reliably identifies *where to start walking*, and reliably misidentifies *what to fix* — which is why both of these would have led a reader straight to the wrong file. The regex looks like the bug. The memsearch code looks like the bug.

The practical consequence is a rule about ordering: walk the dependency chain downward from the error before reading any implementation. For memsearch that chain is short and cheap — is Docker up, is Milvus healthy, does a trivial search return, does a scheduled task already hold the lock — and in both 2026-10-03 cases checking it cost less than reading the code would have. A second, subtler consequence concerns exit codes and generic failures: `memsearch-drain.ps1` exiting 1 after a twenty-minute wait is not a crash but a second run losing the indexing lock, and a reaped background job is a resource event. Both are *correct* behavior reported through a channel that can only express failure. Treating a generic failure signal as a question — what else was true at that moment? — rather than as an answer is what separates the five-minute diagnosis from the afternoon spent debugging a healthy component.

- 2026-10-03 (07:58): "Docker Desktop down ⇒ Milvus down ⇒ memsearch hooks fail with gRPC errors. First thing to check on a memsearch hook failure." Starting Docker restored Milvus to healthy and a test search returned results immediately.

- 2026-10-03 (18:16): "this laptop's Python defaults to CP1252, so Chrome's UTF-8 output fails to decode, stdout comes back `None`, and the regex then errors." The surfaced error was the regex, three statements downstream of the decode.
- 2026-09-30: a memsearch timeout traced to a stopped Docker Milvus container, establishing that "timeouts are nearly uninformative about cause, so check the dependency chain first."
- 2026-09-24: a background job's termination notification was a memory-pressure reap, "a resource event, not a failure to debug."

# Running an Off-Schedule Capture After Proving Nothing Was Missed

The weekly Big 12 forecast capture is specified to run on Wednesdays, and the 2026-09-30 slot was missed. On 2026-10-02 it was run on a Friday anyway, but only after establishing that the deviation cost nothing: no Big 12 games were played between 9/26 and 10/2, so no Week 5 result fell inside the gap. The last capture before this one was 9/23, and the run was justified on the explicit ground that a late capture loses nothing when no state changed in the interval.

## Key Points

- **The schedule exists to protect a property, not to be obeyed.** The Wednesday cadence exists so each capture is a genuine pre-game freeze; what matters is that no games resolved between the scheduled slot and the actual run, which was verified directly rather than assumed.
- **The deviation was argued before it was taken,** with the specific interval named (9/26 to 10/2) and the prior capture dated (9/23), so the reasoning is auditable later rather than appearing as an unexplained Friday entry in the log.
- **A data-integrity check accompanied the run:** 16 of 16 teams, 12 games each, no games appearing or vanishing — confirming the snapshot's shape before any comparison was drawn from it.
- **Grading was reported with its misses, not just its hits.** Week 4: correct winner in 6 of 8 games, with Baylor 23-13 over Colorado hitting the 10-point margin exactly; misses were Kansas State over Cincinnati (Cincinnati won 31-26) and West Virginia at 67% against Oklahoma State (Oklahoma State won 41-24, a 27-point miss).
- **The next slot was re-anchored to the schedule, not to the deviation:** Wednesday 10/7, Mac only, recorded in `docs/STATUS.md` rather than left in the session transcript.

## Details

The transferable judgment is that a cadence is a proxy for a condition, and when the condition can be checked directly the proxy becomes negotiable. For a pre-game forecast freeze the condition is that the capture precedes the games it forecasts — the property that [[connections/hindsight-leakage-and-pregame-freeze-capture]] identifies as the only thing making a retrodictive dataset trustworthy. A Wednesday slot is a convenient way to guarantee that property every week, but it is not the property itself. Checking that no Big 12 games were played in the 9/26–10/2 window establishes the condition held, which is strictly stronger evidence than "we ran on the scheduled day." The inverse case is the one that makes this discipline load-bearing rather than permissive: had any game resolved in the gap, the late capture would have been contaminated and the correct action would have been to record the slot as lost rather than fill it.

Pairing the off-schedule run with a shape check and an honest grading report is what keeps the deviation from quietly degrading the dataset. The 16-teams/12-games verification confirms the snapshot is comparable to its predecessors before any movement is computed from it, which matters because the most interesting outputs of the run were deltas: expected-win movers against the 9/23 baseline (Oklahoma State +1.86, UCF +1.57, Cincinnati +1.20, Utah +1.00 up; West Virginia −1.33, Kansas State −1.32, Colorado −1.06, Iowa State −1.03 down) and probability swings (Oklahoma State vs Kansas State in week 10 up 33 points to 58%, Houston vs Kansas State in week 6 up 25 points to 58%, Utah vs BYU in week 10 up 25 points to 63%). SportScienceResearchRepo maintains a `papers.json` database of sports-science research papers, built up through an ongoing batch-import campaign that processes a large backlog of football-related PDFs in rounds. # Statistical Inference Audit Checklist for Evidence Briefs

The 2026-09-18 adversarial audit of the TOS evidence brief surfaced a reusable set of inferential error patterns that recur whenever a literature review is turned into practice recommendations. The unifying diagnosis was that sources and study-level numbers were largely correct while the *last inferential step* — from observation to causal, screening, or policy claim — was not. The patterns below function as a checklist for auditing any similar brief.

## Key Points

- **Descriptive → causal/screening drift.** The dominant failure: a correlational or descriptive finding is restated as a reason to screen, intervene, or set policy. Check every recommendation against what its cited study design can actually license.
- **"No significant difference" ≠ equivalence.** A null significance test in a small, non-equivalence-designed trial (the cited tennis study had n=10) establishes only that the study lacked power to detect a difference. It is not a safety finding and cannot exonerate an exposure.
- **Reliability/normative data ≠ screening validity.** Datasets establishing that a measure is consistent (pec minor length, DNF, SME, CKCUEST, UQYBT) say nothing about whether that measure predicts the condition of interest.
- **Same-cohort derivation and testing invalidates a cut-point.** An n=49 threshold derived and then tested in the same cohort, with a relative-risk CI of 1.28–68.49, is not a validated screen; the CI width alone signals near-zero information about effect size.
- **Denominator and magnitude hygiene.** Do not juxtapose incompatible denominators (annual incidence vs. 7-year cumulative prevalence). Recompute rhetorical magnitude claims: "four orders of magnitude" for 8.6% vs. 0.004% is actually ~3.33 (ratio ≈ 2,143).
- **Borrowed population rates cannot be applied and then waived.** Using a general-population incidence for an athlete cohort and then dismissing the implication is incoherent — either use an athlete-specific model or state that the expected rate is unknown.

## Details

Two of the patterns deserve particular attention because they are easy to state backwards. The first is the cluster-plausibility argument. Under a Poisson model with the brief's own assumed 4/100,000/yr incidence, a 35-athlete season gives λ = 0.0014, so P(≥2 cases) ≈ 0.000000979 — meaning the model the brief invoked to reassure actually implies the observed two-case cluster is extraordinary. The brief then compounded this by placing a confidence interval around the *observed* event count and using its width as evidence of plausibility; a CI on observed events characterizes uncertainty in the estimate, not surprisingness under an assumed rate, so it answers a different question than the one posed. When a reassurance argument is constructed post hoc, it is worth checking whether the model actually supports the reassurance or contradicts it.

The second is the use of a study design outside the inferential range it supports. A cross-sectional biopsy taken *after* disease onset cannot establish what did or did not cause the disease, yet it was used to exonerate the weight room as a contributing exposure — a temporality violation that no amount of sample size fixes. The same class of error underlies the reliability-as-validity mistake: the studies are real and well-conducted, but they answer "is this measurement repeatable?" rather than "does this measurement predict TOS?", and only the latter licenses a screen. The practical audit procedure that surfaced all of these is a claim-by-claim verification table: for each assertion in the document, record the source, the number as stated in the source, the number as stated in the brief, and — critically — whether the study design supports the inferential use being made. Most rows will pass the first three columns; the fourth is where the findings cluster.

tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

A workflow size guideline is configured for this session: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale.

script.description: Self-contained workflow script. Must begin with `export const meta = { name, description, phases }` (pure literal, no computed values) followed by the script body using agent()/parallel()/pipeline()/phase().

name.description: Name of a predefined workflow (built-in or from .claude/workflows/). Resolves to a self-contained script.

description.description: Ignored — set the workflow description in the script's `meta` block.

title.description: Ignored — set the workflow title in the script's `meta` block.

args.description: Optional input value exposed to the script as the global `args`, verbatim. Pass arrays/objects as actual JSON values, NOT as a JSON-encoded string — a stringified list breaks `args.filter`/`args.map` in the script. Use for parameterized named workflows (e.g. a research question).

scriptPath.description: Path to a workflow script file on disk. Every Workflow invocation persists its script under the session directory and returns the path in the tool result. To iterate, edit that file with Write/Edit and re-invoke Workflow with the same `scriptPath` instead of re-sending the full script. Takes precedence over `script` and `name`.

resumeFromRunId.description: Run ID of a prior Workflow invocation to resume from. Completed agent() calls with unchanged (prompt, opts) return their cached results instantly; only edited or new calls re-run. Same-session only. Stop the prior run first (TaskStop) before resuming.
